analysis.evidence: The battle account continues from Genesis 14:8. Here אֵת introduces כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר, the first of the four opposing kings. The verse restates the matchup as אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים אֶת־הַחֲמִשָּׁה, “four kings against the five.”
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition without a prefix or pronominal suffix.
analysis.sense: Introduces the opposing side in battle.

draft.change: Add Genesis 14:17 as evidence for the two-part spelling of the name.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:17 writes כְּדָר לָעֹמֶר in two parts for the king named כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר in Genesis 14:1.

analysis.evidence: The title מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם, “king of Elam,” immediately follows כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר and identifies him as the first of the four kings listed in Genesis 14:9.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal proper noun with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 69128:1, 69122:4, 69122:8, 69122:11, 69122:14, 69121:3, 69121:6, 69121:9, 69121:12.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם identifies Chedorlaomer as king of Elam, just as אַמְרָפֶל מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר identifies Amraphel as king of Shinar.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun without prefix or suffix. It completes the construct phrase מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם, “king of Elam.”
analysis.sense: Elam, the kingdom ruled by Chedorlaomer

draft.change: Add Genesis 14:9 as evidence for the existing identification.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:9 repeats the name and title וְתִדְעָל מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם from Genesis 14:1.

analysis.evidence: Genesis 14:9 lists four kings by name and title. The title מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם immediately follows וְתִדְעָל, identifying the same king named in Genesis 14:1. The text gives no support for the proposed root תבנ.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ “and” prefixes the personal name תִּדְעָל. The initial ת lacks dagesh after the vocalized prefix.

analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Append the proper noun גּוֹיִם under גוה and assign it the Goyim key already identified in the article’s note.
draft.definition: Goyim is the designation of Tidal’s realm in his royal title.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:1 places Goyim alongside Shinar, Ellasar, and Elam in a list of royal titles. Genesis 14:9 repeats Tidal’s title.

analysis.evidence: The verse names four kings and pairs each with his realm. Goyim follows Tidal’s title מֶלֶךְ in the same position as Elam, Shinar, and Ellasar in the other titles. Genesis 14:1 gives Tidal the same title.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with a plural ending. It completes the construct phrase מֶלֶךְ גּוֹיִם, “king of Goyim.”

draft.change: Add Genesis 14:9 as evidence identifying the same bearer.
draft.definition: Amraphel, the king of Shinar. The meaning of his name is unknown.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:9 repeats the name and royal title found in Genesis 14:1.

analysis.evidence: The title מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר immediately follows וְאַמְרָפֶל and identifies Amraphel as king of Shinar, just as in Genesis 14:1. The verse gives no evidence for deriving the name from אמר.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ joins the personal name אַמְרָפֶל to the preceding names in the list of kings.

analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a place-name entry for Shinar under its own consonants. The source gloss “ewe” and proposed root שנס lack support here.
draft.definition: Shinar is the land in which Genesis 10:10 locates Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh.
draft.evidence: The phrase בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר identifies the region containing the four cities.

analysis.evidence: מֶלֶךְ שִׁנְעָר identifies the land Amraphel rules, just as מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם identifies the land Chedorlaomer rules.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It follows the construct noun מֶלֶךְ in the title “king of Shinar.”
analysis.sense: The land containing Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh.

draft.change: Add Genesis 14:9 as a second attestation of the same bearer.
draft.definition: Arioch, the personal name of the king of Ellasar. Its meaning is uncertain.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:9 repeats the name and royal title אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר from Genesis 14:1.

analysis.evidence: The title מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר identifies Arioch as king of Ellasar. He is the fourth ruler named before the verse counts אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים, “four kings.”
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ־ joins the personal name אַרְיוֹךְ to the preceding list of kings.
Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a place-name entry with the gloss “Ellasar” and correct the source gloss “emptiness; vanity.”
draft.definition: Ellasar is the place named as Arioch’s realm in Genesis 14:1.
draft.evidence: The title אַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר identifies Arioch as king of Ellasar.

analysis.evidence: וְאַרְיוֹךְ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּסָר means “and Arioch, king of Ellasar.” Like עֵילָם and שִׁנְעָר after מֶלֶךְ in the same list, אֶלָּסָר names a king’s realm.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים means “four kings.” It counts the four kings just named and sets them against הַחֲמִשָּׁה, “the five.”
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute cardinal numeral modifying the masculine plural noun מְלָכִים.

analysis.evidence: אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים means “four kings.” It counts the four rulers just named, each introduced with the title מֶלֶךְ.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute of the common noun מֶלֶךְ, with no prefix or pronominal suffix.

analysis.evidence: אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים אֶת הַחֲמִשָּׁה summarizes the battle as “four kings against the five.” The complement הַחֲמִשָּׁה identifies the five opposing kings.
analysis.morphology: Simple preposition with no prefix or pronominal suffix.
analysis.sense: with, marking the opposing side in battle

analysis.evidence: In אַרְבָּעָה מְלָכִים אֶת הַחֲמִשָּׁה, “four kings against the five,” מְלָכִים supplies the understood noun for הַחֲמִשָּׁה.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes the masculine singular absolute form of the cardinal numeral. The numeral stands for the five kings.
